title: Inversion for emphasis
objective: Add emphasis and formality with negative and restrictive adverbials: Never have I…, Not only…, Hardly… when.

sections.heading: How inversion works
sections.en: After a negative or restrictive expression at the start of a sentence, use question word order: auxiliary + subject + verb. If there is no auxiliary, add do / does / did.
sections.fr: Registre soutenu : essais, discours, IELTS Writing band 7+. À doser : une ou deux fois par texte.
examples: Never have I seen such a crowd.
Rarely does the government admit its mistakes.
Not only did she pass, but she also won a prize.

sections.heading: Common triggers
sections.en: Use these at the start of the sentence.
table: Seldom do we get a second chance.
Not only is it cheap, but it's also fast.
Hardly had I arrived when it started to rain.
No sooner had we left than the bus broke down.
Only after the test did I relax.
Under no circumstances should you share your password.

sections.heading: Conditionals without if
sections.en: Formal writing replaces if with inversion: Had I known… / Should you need help… / Were it not for…
examples: Should you have any questions, please contact us.
Were it not for her support, I would have given up.

vocab.definition: not often (formal)
vocab.example: Seldom have I read such a clear report.

vocab.definition: a fact or condition that affects a situation
vocab.example: Under no circumstances should you leave early.

vocab.definition: never having happened before
vocab.example: The city saw unprecedented growth.

vocab.definition: to accept or admit that something is true
vocab.example: Rarely do leaders acknowledge their errors.

practice.explanation: Never + auxiliary + subject: have I seen.

practice.prompt: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the slides.
practice.explanation: No auxiliary in the original → add did: did he arrive.

quiz.prompt: Rarely ___ such dedication.
Hardly had I sat down ___ the phone rang.
___ you need further information, please call us. (formal 'if', 6 letters)
quiz.explanation: Should you need = If you need (formal).

quiz.prompt: "Under no circumstances you should open this door" is correct.
quiz.explanation: Inversion needed: Under no circumstances should you open…

quiz.prompt: No sooner had we arrived ___ it began to snow.
___ it not for the rain, we would have won.
quiz.explanation: Were it not for = If it were not for.

quiz.prompt: Put the words in order.
quiz.answer: Only then did I understand the problem

rememberErrors.why: Add do/does/did when there is no auxiliary.

title: Hedging and academic stance
objective: Express precise degrees of certainty, as expected in academic writing and IELTS band 7+.

sections.heading: Why hedge?
sections.en: Academic writers rarely claim absolute truth. Hedging shows you are careful and credible: it would appear that, this may suggest, to a certain extent, arguably.
sections.fr: Trop d'affirmations catégoriques (always, never, prove) font perdre des points en écriture académique.

sections.heading: Tools for hedging
sections.en: Choose the strength you mean.
examples: These findings suggest a link between sleep and memory.
Remote work tends to increase productivity, at least in some sectors.
table: to some extent, in most cases, there is evidence that

sections.heading: Boosting and stance
sections.en: When the evidence is strong, boost carefully: clearly, undoubtedly, it is evident that. Stance adverbs show your attitude: Surprisingly, Regrettably, Interestingly.
examples: Interestingly, the effect disappears after six months.
It is evident that further research is needed.

vocab.definition: used to say something may be true, with good reasons
vocab.fr: sans doute, on peut soutenir que
vocab.example: This is arguably the best solution.

vocab.definition: to usually do or be something
vocab.example: Older users tend to prefer phone calls.

vocab.definition: the results of research
vocab.example: The findings were published last year.

vocab.definition: partly, not completely
vocab.example: I agree with this view to some extent.

vocab.definition: seeming likely to be true
vocab.example: This is a plausible explanation.

options: This proves that social media causes depression.
This may suggest a link between social media and low mood.
Everyone knows social media is bad.

quiz.prompt: 'The results ___ that the method works.' (cautious)
quiz.explanation: indicate is cautious; prove is too strong.

quiz.prompt: 'Seeming likely to be true' is…
Hedging means making stronger, absolute claims.
Young people ___ spend more time online. (usually)
The ___ of the study were surprising. (results, 8 letters)
Which is a stance adverb?

title: Cleft sentences for focus
objective: Highlight the key information in speech and writing with it-clefts and what-clefts.

sections.heading: It-clefts
sections.en: It + be + focused part + that/who + rest. Use them to correct or contrast.
examples: It was Ama who found the solution (not Kofi).
It's the cost that worries me, not the distance.
It wasn't until 2020 that I started English.

sections.heading: What-clefts
sections.en: What + clause + be + focus. Great for presenting your main point or a need.
examples: What I need is more practice.
What surprised me was how friendly everyone was.
What you should do is contact the embassy.

sections.heading: Other focusing structures
sections.en: All (that) I want is… · The reason (why)… is that… · The thing that… is…
examples: All I want is a quiet place to study.
The reason I'm applying is that I love research.

vocab.definition: to show that something is especially important
vocab.example: I'd like to emphasise one point.

vocab.definition: extremely important
vocab.example: What is crucial is the first impression.

vocab.definition: real but not obvious
vocab.example: The underlying problem is poor planning.

practice.prompt: ___ I really need is a break.
It was in Accra ___ we first met.

quiz.prompt: It wasn't until midnight ___ he called.
What annoys me ___ the noise.
___ I want is a quiet room. (3 letters, = the only thing)
"It was Kofi who broke the window" emphasises who did it.
The reason I left ___ that the salary was low.
Put the words in order.
quiz.answer: What matters most is your attitude

rememberErrors.wrong: What I need it is time.

title: Presentations and debates
objective: Structure a presentation, handle questions and disagree diplomatically in seminars and meetings.

sections.heading: Signposting
sections.en: Guide your audience: I'd like to begin by… · Moving on to… · This brings me to… · To sum up…
sections.fr: Les « signposts » rendent un exposé facile à suivre — critère clé en entretien et en master.
examples: I'd like to begin by outlining the problem.
This brings me to my second point.
To wrap up, let me highlight three key takeaways.

sections.heading: Handling questions
sections.en: Buy time and stay in control: That's a great question. · If I understand you correctly, you're asking… · I'm afraid I don't have the figures to hand, but I'll get back to you.
examples: That's a fair point — let me come back to it at the end.
I'd rather not speculate, but the data suggest…

sections.heading: Disagreeing diplomatically
sections.en: Soften disagreement: I see your point, but… · I'm not entirely convinced that… · With respect, I'd argue that…
sections.fr: Évitez « You're wrong ». Le désaccord poli est attendu à C1.

vocab.definition: to give the main ideas without details
vocab.example: Let me outline the plan.

vocab.definition: a key idea people should remember
vocab.example: The main takeaway is: practise daily.

vocab.definition: available, near you
vocab.example: I don't have the numbers to hand.

vocab.definition: completely sure
vocab.example: I'm not entirely convinced.

options: I'm not entirely convinced that's the case.

practice.prompt: To move to the next part:
options: This brings me to my next point.

quiz.prompt: When you don't know the answer:
options: I'm afraid I don't have that to hand, but I'll get back to you.

quiz.prompt: Let me ___ the main ideas. (give without details)
"To sum up" introduces the conclusion.
A key idea to remember is a…
"With respect, I'd argue that…" is used to…

rememberErrors.right: I see your point, but I'd argue that…

rememberErrors.wrong: I will talk about three things. First thing…

title: Subjunctive and unreal past
objective: Use formal subjunctive and the unreal past after wish, it's time, would rather and as if.

sections.heading: The formal subjunctive
sections.en: After verbs and adjectives of demand or importance (suggest, insist, recommend, essential, vital), use the base form for all persons — no -s, no should needed.
sections.fr: « Il est essentiel qu'il soit présent » = It is essential that he be present.
examples: The committee recommends that she be promoted.
It is vital that every student submit the form.
I insist that he apologise.

sections.heading: Unreal past
sections.en: Use a past form for a present unreal meaning after: It's (high) time…, I'd rather you…, as if / as though, suppose / supposing.
examples: It's high time we made a decision.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
He talks as if he were the boss.
Suppose you lost your passport — what would you do?

vocab.definition: to demand firmly
vocab.example: She insisted that he leave.

vocab.definition: extremely important and urgent
vocab.example: It is imperative that we act now.

vocab.definition: a group chosen to make decisions
vocab.example: The committee met on Monday.

practice.prompt: The doctor recommended that he ___ more water.

quiz.prompt: It is essential that everyone ___ on time.
I'd rather you ___ smoke here.
He acts as if he ___ the owner. (be, formal)
"They insisted that she pays" is the standard formal form.
It's high time the government ___ action.
___ you won the lottery, what would you buy?

rememberErrors.wrong: It is important that he comes.
rememberErrors.right: It is important that he come.

title: Idioms and phrasal verbs at work
objective: Understand and use common idioms and phrasal verbs from offices, meetings and media.

sections.heading: Idioms you will hear
sections.en: Learn idioms in context; don't overuse them in formal essays.
sections.fr: Les idiomes rapportent des points à l'oral (IELTS Speaking), beaucoup moins à l'écrit académique.
table: do something badly to save time or money

sections.heading: Phrasal verbs for work
sections.en: come up with (an idea) · carry out (research) · point out (a fact) · run out of (time) · put forward (a proposal) · follow up (on).
examples: She came up with a brilliant solution.
We ran out of time before the last question.
I'll follow up on this by email.

vocab.definition: to think of an idea or plan
vocab.example: He came up with a new strategy.

vocab.definition: to do a task, research or plan
vocab.example: They carried out a survey.

vocab.definition: to do something cheaply or carelessly
vocab.example: Don't cut corners on safety.

vocab.definition: a situation where you must learn a lot fast
vocab.example: My first month abroad was a steep learning curve.

practice.prompt: We had no more time: we ___ time.

quiz.prompt: 'The most important fact' is…
She came ___ with a great idea. (2 letters)
To 'cut corners' is a good professional practice.
quiz.explanation: It means doing things carelessly to save time/money.

quiz.prompt: The researchers ___ a survey of 500 students.
'Are we on the same page?' asks if we…
quiz.explanation: on the same page = in agreement.

rememberErrors.wrong: We need to cut the corners.

rememberErrors.right: He came up with an idea.

title: Nominalisation for formal writing
objective: Turn verbs and adjectives into nouns to write in a concise, academic style.

sections.heading: What is nominalisation?
sections.en: Academic English often expresses actions as nouns: 'Prices increased rapidly' → 'The rapid increase in prices'. It sounds more objective and packs more information into a sentence.
sections.fr: Très utile en IELTS Task 1 (graphiques) et dans les essais.

sections.heading: Rewriting sentences
sections.en: Move the action into a noun phrase and choose a neutral verb (lead to, result in, cause, contribute to).
examples: Because the government invested more, unemployment fell. → Greater government investment led to a fall in unemployment.
People are becoming aware of climate change. → There is growing awareness of climate change.

vocab.definition: knowledge that something exists or is important
vocab.example: Public awareness of the issue is growing.

vocab.definition: to be one of the causes of
vocab.example: Stress contributes to poor sleep.

vocab.definition: a gradual decrease
vocab.example: There was a sharp decline in sales.

quiz.prompt: The noun of 'fail' is…
'Investment rose, so jobs increased.' → Higher investment ___ more jobs.
able → ___ (noun)
Nominalisation usually makes writing more formal and concise.
There was a sharp ___ in unemployment. (it went down)
The noun of 'important' is…

rememberErrors.right: This led to problems. / This leads to problems.

title: Ellipsis and substitution
objective: Avoid repetition like a native speaker with so, not, do so, one(s) and ellipsis.

sections.heading: so and not
sections.en: Replace a whole clause after think, hope, expect, suppose, be afraid: I think so / I hope not / I'm afraid not.
sections.fr: « Je pense que oui » = I think so (pas « I think yes »).
examples: Will it rain? — I hope not.
Is he coming? — I suppose so.
Did you pass? — I'm afraid not.

sections.heading: do so, one(s), auxiliaries
sections.en: do (so) replaces a verb phrase; one / ones replaces a countable noun; an auxiliary alone avoids repeating the verb.
examples: She promised to call, and she did so.
I prefer the blue shirt to the red one.
I can't swim, but my sister can.
He said he'd finish it, and he has.

sections.heading: Ellipsis
sections.en: Leave out words that are obvious from context, especially after and, but, or to.
examples: I wanted to go, but I didn't have time to.
She can speak French and (she can speak) Ewe.

vocab.definition: to think something is probably true
vocab.example: I suppose so.

vocab.definition: saying the same thing again
vocab.example: Avoid repetition in your essay.

practice.prompt: Is the shop open? — I think ___.
I like the big bag, not the small ___.
practice.explanation: one replaces a singular countable noun.

quiz.prompt: Will it be expensive? — I hope ___.
These shoes are nicer than the old ___.
I can't drive, but my brother ___. (auxiliary)
"I think yes" is natural English.
He asked me to leave, and I ___.
quiz.explanation: do so replaces the verb phrase.

quiz.prompt: I meant to call you, but I forgot ___.
quiz.explanation: Ellipsis after to: I forgot to.

rememberErrors.why: Use so to replace the clause.

rememberErrors.right: I don't think so. / I think not.
